mots.sens: This term refers to a military commander or general, often associated with acts of conquest. In the biblical context, it evokes authority and military power, highlighting the threat that Assyria posed to Israel. Spiritually, it reminds us that the forces of evil may seem triumphant, but God remains sovereign over all nations.

This word refers to Assyria, a nation known for its brutality and territorial expansion. Assyria is often a symbol of divine judgment in the Scriptures, representing the consequences of Israel's sin. Theologically, this illustrates how God even uses pagan nations to accomplish His purposes.

Asdod was one of the five main cities of the Philistines, symbolizing resistance to divine authority. The capture of this city by the Assyrians underscores the vulnerability of nations before God's will. It reminds us that places of resistance to God can be subjected to His judgment.

1.epoque: This passage is set in the 8th century B.C., during the period when Assyria was a dominant power in the Middle East, threatening neighboring kingdoms, including Israel and Judah.
1.passage: Isaiah 20 is part of a series of prophecies where the prophet announces God's judgment on the nations, and this verse introduces a significant historical event that illustrates God's sovereignty over human affairs.
1.culture: In the culture of the time, wars and conquests were often seen as manifestations of divine will, and the capture of cities was a sign of God's favor or judgment upon a people.
1.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse reminds us that even the most tragic historical events are under God's control. The capture of Asdod by the Assyrians serves as a warning to Israel regarding the consequences of its unfaithfulness to God.
1.commentaire: This passage teaches us that God uses even difficult events to accomplish His purposes. As believers, we must remain vigilant and faithful, knowing that even in times of adversity, God is at work to fulfill His plan. This encourages us to place our trust in Him, even when circumstances seem desperate.

mots.sens: The Hebrew word 'sac' (שׂ) refers to a garment made of coarse cloth, often used to symbolize mourning or humility. In this context, it represents a condition of repentance and spiritual distress. The act of loosening the sack from the loins indicates a relinquishing of material concerns to focus on the divine call.

The term 'nu' (עָרוּם) evokes the idea of being stripped, both physically and spiritually. This can symbolize vulnerability before God and a nakedness of the heart. In this verse, walking naked and barefoot emphasizes the necessity of presenting oneself before God without pretense, in complete transparency.

The word 'parole' (דְּבַר) is central to divine communication, representing God's authority and revelation. In this passage, the word of the Lord to Isaiah underscores the importance of obedience to God's voice. It reminds us that every divine instruction is an invitation to act according to His will.

2.epoque: This passage is set during the period of the kings of Israel and Judah, a time marked by idolatry and external threats, particularly from the Assyrians.
2.passage: Isaiah 20 is part of a series of prophecies where God uses symbolic actions to convey powerful messages to the people, here concerning the imminent judgment on Egypt and Ethiopia.
2.culture: In Hebrew culture, the act of undressing or wearing sackcloth was often associated with signs of mourning, repentance, or prophecy, serving to capture the people's attention regarding spiritual realities.
2.interpretation: This passage illustrates God's radical call to His prophets to live out spiritual truths in tangible ways. Isaiah, by acting in this manner, becomes a living symbol of God's message regarding the shame and impending defeat of the nations that oppose Him.
2.commentaire: Isaiah's obedience to the divine instruction, even in such a humiliating form, reminds us that God may ask for personal sacrifices for His work. This passage encourages us to be sensitive to God's voice and to respond in faith, even when it pushes us out of our comfort zone. As believers, we are called to shed burdens and distractions to fully dedicate ourselves to the mission God entrusts to us.

mots.sens: This word means 'servant' and is often used to designate a person in a position of submission or devotion. In the context of Isaiah, it underscores the relationship of dependence and obedience of God's servant towards the Lord. Spiritually, it reminds us that we are called to be servants of God, acting according to His will and carrying His message to the world.

This term translates to 'sign' or 'omen' and implies a divine indication or miracle with particular significance. In this passage, it is used to signal a future event that will have repercussions for Egypt and Ethiopia. Theologically, this underscores that God uses signs to communicate with His people and to reveal His plans.

This word means 'naked' and evokes the idea of vulnerability and humility. In the context of Isaiah, walking naked symbolizes an act of despair or judgment. Spiritually, it reminds us that we must strip away our pride and possessions to fully submit to God's will.

This word means 'shoe' and represents protection and preparation for the journey. In this context, walking barefoot indicates a break with conventions and a nakedness before God. Theologically, this can be seen as an invitation to abandon our earthly securities to follow the Lord into the unknown.

3.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the kingdom of Judah, in the 8th century B.C., a period marked by political tensions and military threats from surrounding powers such as Egypt and Assyria.
3.passage: In Isaiah 20, the prophet is called to live a symbolic experience to illustrate God's imminent judgment on Egypt and Ethiopia. This chapter emphasizes the importance of faithfulness to God in the face of external challenges.
3.culture: In the culture of the time, clothing and shoes symbolized status and dignity. Walking naked and barefoot was a provocative act, intended to shock and draw attention to the divine message.
3.interpretation: This verse illustrates how God uses symbolic actions to communicate deep truths. Nakedness and being barefoot represent a call to humility and total dependence on Him, while announcing judgment on the nations.
3.commentaire: The passage of Isaiah 20:3 reminds us that God may call us to actions that seem strange or perplexing, but that have a divine purpose. As believers, we must be ready to obey God, even when it involves giving up our comfort or status. This also invites us to reflect on our own dependence on God and how we witness our faith in a world that does not always understand our choices.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to bear', 'to lift', or 'to carry away'. In this context, it evokes the idea of capturing and taking people away, emphasizing the strength and authority of the king of Assyria. The theological implication here is that God uses nations to fulfill His purposes, even when it involves the suffering and humiliation of His people.

This term means 'slave' or 'servant'. It evokes the condition of those who are captured, highlighting their loss of dignity and their state of vulnerability. Spiritually, it reminds us of humanity's condition without Christ, reduced to the slavery of sin, and the necessity of redemption.

This word means 'glory' or 'honor'. In this passage, it is related to the shame that Egypt will experience, contrasting with the divine glory that should be attributed to God. This shows that nations that oppose God and His people will ultimately be humiliated, underscoring God's sovereignty over all nations.

This verb means 'to be ashamed' or 'to be confused'. The use of this term in the verse highlights the dishonor and humiliation that Egypt will suffer due to its defeat. Theologically, it reminds us that those who oppose God will ultimately be exposed and ashamed, a call to repentance and submission to divine will.

4.epoque: This passage is set in the 8th century B.C., during a period of political and military tensions between the nations of the Near East, particularly between Israel, Egypt, and Assyria.
4.passage: Isaiah 20 is part of a series of prophecies where the prophet Isaiah announces God's judgment on the nations, particularly on Egypt, which had been a source of refuge for Israel. This chapter illustrates the imminent defeat of Egypt at the hands of Assyria.
4.culture: In ancient culture, the capture and humiliation of enemies were often seen as demonstrations of power and victory. Being taken away naked and barefoot was an extreme humiliation, symbolizing the loss of dignity and status.
4.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's sovereignty over the nations and His judgment against those who oppose Him. Spiritually, it reminds us that trust in human powers, like Egypt for Israel, can lead to shame and disappointment when those powers fail.
4.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of placing our trust in God rather than in human alliances. Even in times of distress, God is sovereign and uses events to fulfill His purposes. As believers, we must remember that our true security is found in Christ, who frees us from the slavery of sin and gives us renewed dignity.

mots.sens: This term refers to Ethiopia, a nation often associated with power and wealth in antiquity. In the biblical context, Ethiopia represents a source of trust and hope for Israel, but here it becomes a symbol of disappointment. The root of the word evokes a distant land, emphasizing the idea that trust placed in foreign nations can lead to spiritual disillusionment.

The word refers to Egypt, an emblematic nation in Israel's history, often synonymous with oppression and idolatry. Egypt also represents a source of pride for Israel, but here that pride is called into question. The theological significance of this term underscores the danger of boasting in human alliances rather than trusting in God.

This verb means 'to be embarrassed' or 'to be confused'. It expresses a state of shame and despair in the face of a disappointing situation. In this verse, it illustrates Israel's reaction when it realizes that its trust in Ethiopia and Egypt was misplaced, highlighting the importance of grounding our hope in God alone.

This term means 'to think' or 'to count', and it is often used to describe how people evaluate their options. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the idea that trust in human powers is a faulty evaluation, leading to confusion and fear. It reminds believers of the importance of discerning God's will in their choices.

5.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the 8th century B.C., a period marked by political tensions between neighboring nations and Israel.
5.passage: Isaiah 20 is part of a series of prophecies where the prophet warns Israel of the consequences of its trust in human alliances rather than in God. This chapter illustrates the imminent defeat of Egypt and Ethiopia, and the despair that will result for those who rely on them.
5.culture: In antiquity, nations often sought alliances for protection against invasions. Egypt and Ethiopia were perceived as military powers, and their support was sought by Israel, reflecting a cultural dependence on human powers.
5.interpretation: This verse highlights the fragility of human alliances and the disappointment that follows when one places trust in nations rather than in God. It reminds believers that true sources of security and peace are found only in God.
5.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on the foundations of our trust. As believers, we must avoid relying on human resources or temporary alliances, but rather anchor ourselves in God's promise and faithfulness. In times of uncertainty, let us remember that our true security comes from our relationship with the Lord.

mots.sens: This word means 'expectation' or 'hope'. It evokes the idea of a fervent desire and trust placed in something or someone. In the context of this verse, it underscores the disillusionment of the inhabitants regarding their disappointed expectations concerning the help from the king of Assyria. Spiritually, it reminds us that our true hope must be placed in God, and not in human alliances.

This term means 'rescue' or 'deliverance'. It is often used to describe divine intervention or providential help. In this passage, it highlights the anguish of the inhabitants who realize that their trust in man has left them without help. Theologically, it teaches us that only God can truly deliver us from our oppressions.

This word means 'to be happy' or 'to be secure'. In this context, it emphasizes the quest for security of the inhabitants in the face of the Assyrian threat. It reminds us that true peace is not found in human alliances, but in a relationship with God. Spiritually, it challenges us to seek security in Christ, our true refuge.

6.epoque: This passage is set during the period when the kingdom of Judah is threatened by Assyria, a dominant military power of the time.
6.passage: Isaiah 20 is part of a collection of prophecies where the prophet Isaiah warns the people of Judah not to rely on human alliances for their protection, but to turn to God.
6.culture: At this time, nations often sought alliances for protection against invaders. Trust in human powers was common, but often disappointing.
6.interpretation: This verse illustrates the disillusionment of the coastal inhabitants who realize that their hope placed in the king of Assyria is in vain. It reminds us that any trust in man can lead to disappointment, and that our true help comes from God alone.
6.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of placing our trust in God rather than in human alliances. In times of uncertainty, it is essential to remember that our hope and deliverance come from our relationship with the Lord. It encourages us to seek God in all things, for He is our true refuge and strength.
